content: Dioxins are a group of chemical compounds known as polychlorinated dibenzodioxins (PCDDs), which belong to the family of halogenated organic compounds. These compounds are highly lipophilic, meaning they accumulate in fatty tissues of humans and wildlife. Dioxins are recognized as teratogens (causing birth defects), mutagens (causing genetic mutations), and suspected human carcinogens (cancer-causing agents). The chemical structure of PCDDs consists of two benzene rings connected by a double oxygen bridge. Chlorine atoms can attach to the molecule at eight specific positions (1–4 and 6–9). There are 75 different types of PCDD congeners, but only those with chlorine atoms at positions 2, 3, 7, and 8 are significantly toxic. Of these, only seven congeners are considered toxic under the NATO/CCMS international toxic equivalence (I-TEQ) scheme. Historically, dioxins were present in the environment at lower concentrations before industrialization, primarily due to natural combustion and geological processes. The first intentional synthesis of chlorinated dibenzodioxins occurred in 1872. Today, dioxins are found in all humans, with higher levels in individuals from industrialized regions. The most toxic dioxin, 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD), gained notoriety as a contaminant in Agent Orange, a herbicide used during the Vietnam War. Dioxins have also been linked to environmental contamination incidents in places like Times Beach, Missouri; Love Canal, New York; and Seveso, Italy. More recently, dioxin poisoning was implicated in the 2004 case of Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko. Dioxins primarily enter the human population through the ingestion of food, particularly fish, meat, and dairy products, as they are fat-soluble and bioaccumulate in the food chain. Occupational exposure is a concern for workers in the chemical industry or those handling herbicides. Inhalation exposure can occur near significant point sources of emissions, especially where emission controls are inadequate. In developed nations, regulations have reduced dioxin emissions, but concerns remain about underreporting due to insufficient sampling. For example, continuous sampling in Belgium revealed that periodic sampling underestimated emissions by 30 to 50 times. Dioxins are produced in small amounts during the combustion of organic material in the presence of chlorine, whether as chloride ions or organochlorine compounds. Major sources of dioxin emissions include coal-fired utilities, metal smelting, diesel trucks, land application of sewage sludge, burning treated wood, and trash burn barrels. These sources account for nearly 80% of dioxin emissions. Incineration, once a major source, now contributes less than 3% of emissions due to stringent regulations and improved emission controls. Dioxins can also form during non-combustion processes, such as bleaching fibers for paper or textiles and manufacturing chlorinated phenols. Higher levels of chlorination require higher reaction temperatures, leading to greater dioxin production. Dioxins may also form during the photochemical breakdown of compounds like triclosan and are present in cigarette smoke, though this remains understudied. Dioxins are absorbed primarily through dietary intake of fat, where they accumulate in animals and humans. Highly chlorinated dioxins are stored in fatty tissues and are not easily metabolized or excreted, with half-lives ranging from 8 to 132 years. The persistence of a specific dioxin congener depends on its structure. Dioxins with fewer chlorines are more readily oxidized by cytochrome P450 enzymes, facilitating excretion. TCDD is the most toxic congener, and its toxicity is rated as 1 on the Toxic Equivalence Factor (TEF) scale. TEFs are used internationally to estimate the health risks of dioxin mixtures, but recent data suggest that non-linear toxicity models may be more appropriate for complex mixtures. Dioxins are subject to international regulation under the Stockholm Convention, which obligates signatories to minimize or eliminate dioxin sources. In humans, dioxins bioaccumulate in fatty tissues over time, potentially reaching dangerous levels even with small exposures. The EPA classifies dioxins as probable carcinogens and notes that non-cancer effects, such as reproductive, developmental, and immune system damage, may pose even greater health risks. TCDD has a half-life of approximately 8 years in humans, but elimination rates increase at high concentrations due to enhanced metabolism. Dioxins act on the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) and bioaccumulate in food chains, leading to dangerous concentrations even from small environmental exposures. High levels of dioxin exposure in humans can cause chloracne, a severe form of persistent acne. Other potential effects include developmental abnormalities in children's teeth enamel, nervous system pathology, thyroid disorders, immune system damage, endometriosis, and diabetes. Animal studies have shown that TCDD is teratogenic, mutagenic, carcinogenic, immunotoxic, and hepatotoxic. It also disrupts endocrine and growth factor systems. The most sensitive effects, observed across multiple species, include developmental impacts on the immune, nervous, and reproductive systems. These effects occur at body burdens similar to those reported in humans. In Vietnam, exposure to Agent Orange, heavily contaminated with TCDD, has been linked to birth defects and other disorders in both U.S. veterans and the Vietnamese population. TCDD levels in some U.S. veterans were up to 600 parts per trillion (ppt) years after exposure, compared to 1–2 ppt in the general population. In Vietnam, TCDD levels in contaminated soil and sediments have reached up to 1,000,000 ppt decades after spraying. Elevated levels have also been found in food and wildlife. Several notable dioxin exposure incidents have occurred, including industrial accidents, contamination of food chains, and environmental disasters. For example, in 1976, a large dioxin release occurred in Seveso, Italy, leading to widespread contamination. In 1999, a dioxin crisis in Belgium resulted from contaminated animal feed, leading to the slaughter of millions of chickens and pigs. On September 11, 2001, explosions released massive amounts of dust containing dioxins, with ambient concentrations reported as some of the highest ever recorded. Individual cases of dioxin poisoning, such as the 2004 poisoning of Viktor Yushchenko, highlight the severe health effects of high-dose exposure. In one case, a woman exposed to the highest recorded dose of dioxin experienced chloracne, nausea, vomiting, and other symptoms but showed relatively normal immune function tests. Another individual exposed to a lower dose suffered only from chloracne. These cases underscore the variability in individual responses to dioxin exposure.
